passage:
"So how did the chess match go?" Urmila asked, ladling dal.
"I crushed Kunal! Checkmate in twenty moves! I told him to stick to snakes and ladders." Sumit grinned.
"You said that to his face?"
"Everyone laughed."
"Did Kunal?"
Sumit stopped, spoon halfway up. "No. He left early. He didn't even look at me."
"Was it sweet?"
"For a minute. Then kind of empty. Ishaan didn't clap either."
"You may play Kunal again, beta."
"He might beat me next time."
"And what would you want him to do then?"
Sumit put down his spoon. "Say well played. I'll tell him that tomorrow. 😊"

qa.q: How many moves did Sumit say the checkmate took?
What was Sumit feeling when Urmila asked whether Kunal laughed?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and a little ashamed: Sumit stopped with the spoon halfway and admitted the win felt empty.

qa.q: What could Sumit do tomorrow to repair things with Kunal?
qa.a: Tell Kunal "well played," as Sumit says will happen.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt when Sumit teased him?
qa.a: Hurt and embarrassed, since he left early and did not look at Sumit.

grounding: After beating a rival, the child shows off and rubs it in, finds it sweet for a moment but empty, and resolves to be gracious.

passage:
"Kalyani, checkmate!"
"Well played, Shankar."
"Well played? I destroyed you! Twelve moves. You should stick to ludo."
"Okay. You won."
"Admit it. You're rubbish."
Kalyani stood up. "I said you won. I'm not saying I'm rubbish."
She walked off. Shankar laughed and looked round. But his friend Moin was frowning.
"What?"
"That was mean. She beat you last month, and she didn't say anything like that."
Shankar's grin faded. "I was just excited."
"Excited doesn't need to be mean. Next time she might win again."
Shankar looked at the board. Then he went to find Kalyani.

qa.q: How many moves did Shankar say he won in?
How did Shankar feel when Moin frowned?
qa.a: He felt caught out and uncomfortable, his grin fading.

qa.q: What would a more gracious response have been?
qa.a: Accepting Kalyani's "well played" warmly and saying something kind, like she did when she beat him last month.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel after Shankar's gloating?
qa.a: Kalyani felt hurt and disrespected, walking away after being called rubbish.

grounding: A boy beats his rival and rubs it in; a friend points out it costs respect and that next time he may lose, prompting him to go back.

passage:
I'm Jyoti. In Class 6, I beat Jasleen in the school spelling bee. We'd been rivals all year.
I didn't just win. I danced around the stage and said, "Better luck next time, Jasleen!" loud enough for everyone. My friends laughed.
It felt sweet for about a day. Then I noticed people looking at me differently. A teacher said, "Winning well matters too."
Next term, Jasleen beat me in the inter-house quiz. She just shook my hand and said, "You made me work hard."
I went home and felt small. She had been so gracious, and I hadn't. After that I tried to be more like her.

qa.q: What competition did Jyoti win against Jasleen?
How did Jyoti feel after Jasleen was gracious in the quiz?
qa.a: Jyoti felt small and ashamed, realising the gloating had cost respect.

qa.q: What did Jyoti learn from Jasleen?
qa.a: That winning or losing graciously matters more, because next time you might lose.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt when Jyoti danced and teased her?
qa.a: Jasleen probably felt hurt and embarrassed in front of everyone.

grounding: Jyoti beats a rival and rubs it in, loses respect, then loses to the rival, who is gracious, and learns to be gracious too.
